 JUNCTION CITY, Ore. — Identity theft is costing older Americans tens of millions of dollars, and one Junction City woman said she learned just how damaging it can be when student loans were taken out in her name.
 According to the 2025 FBI Internet Crime Report, senior Americans lost more than $48 million in just one year to identity theft, a number that’s only climbing.
 Nancy Plemons, a 71-year-old retired educator and Junction City resident, said she was shocked when she received a letter from a university she didn’t recognize saying she owed nearly $5,000 in student loans.
 “Somebody had taken my information and got not one but two student loans from EdFinancial,” Plemons said.
 Plemons said the loans dropped her credit by more than 100 points and led to months of sleepless nights. She said the Virginia-based Strayer University would not disclose what classes she was supposedly paying for, even after verifying she was the real Nancy Plemons.
 “I could not get anybody to listen to me. It was, ‘Send this documentation, send this documentation, send this documentation.’ So I did,” she said.
 Plemons said Strayer only agreed to close its account after she told the school she had contacted the news media. The university did not respond to a request for comment or an opportunity to dispute that claim.
 “Okay, not one word of apology for the six, seven, eight months of agony that I have spent over all of this,” Plemons said.
 Plemons said EdFinancial still holds her responsible for the loans. The servicer did not respond to a request for comment either.
 Lane Thompson, Oregon’s student loan ombudsman, said federal borrowers who are victims of fraud can apply to have fraudulent loans discharged.
 “The first thing that they’re going to want to do is go onto the StudentAid.gov website. In this case, they would want to find the ID theft or fraud discharge application, complete that, and send it to their servicer,” Thompson said.
 While Plemons’ age may not have been a factor in her case, the FBI says older adults can be attractive targets to scammers because they may have savings and be more trusting or lonely than younger individuals.
 Alexandra Hunter, an adult protective services specialist, said loneliness is a major factor she commonly sees among scam victims.
 Identity thieves take out two student loans in Junction City retiree's name 
 “Because after so long working in this field and talking to so many victims, one of the common denominators I’ve noticed is loneliness,” Hunter said.
 If someone suspects they have been a victim of fraud or a scam, Hunter recommends immediately contacting financial institutions, changing passwords and freezing credit. She also encouraged older adults to seek help and said Adult Protective Services can connect people with resources, including companionship and support groups.
 “If you’re scared to talk about it with your peers, call Adult Protective Services. We can hook you up with somebody, maybe a senior companion, maybe a support group,” Hunter said.
